title: B-T-Ch

lines: A CHEST OF JEWELS, FULL OF DIRT.
THIS TOO IS FOR THE GOOD.
cards: A man in the Talmud goes by Nachum Ish Gamzu, and his nickname is a sentence. Whatever happened to him, he would say gam zu l'tovah: this too is for the good.
Once, the story goes, he was sent to the emperor with a chest of jewels as a gift. At an inn on the way, the chest was emptied in the night and filled with dirt.

He arrived, opened it before the emperor, and there was only earth. The Talmud tells how the dirt turned out to be useful after all, and he came home honored. Whatever you make of the ending, the man had a habit.

teach.b: B-T-Ch. Bet, tet, chet. Bitachon: trust.
First, the verb. Proverbs puts it plainly: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding."
Trust is something you do, and the verse sets it against leaning on your own reading of events.
Second, the same letters mean safety. Leviticus promises that if the people keep the commandments, "ye shall dwell in the land in safety." The Hebrew is la-vetach, from this root.

And a psalm uses it at bedtime: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." Trusting and being safe live under one roof. Trust is somewhere you can lie down.
The Jewish philosopher Bachya ibn Pakuda wrote Duties of the Heart, and one of its gates is the gate of trust.
He treats trust as work done inside, by the heart, while a person still does their part in the world. Fourth, back to Nachum. Jewish thinkers have argued about what bitachon expects.

teach.h: TRUST IS SOMEWHERE TO LIE DOWN.
teach.b: Some teach that it means confidence that things will turn out well. Others teach that it means confidence that whatever comes is held by God, even when it doesn't look good. Nachum's sentence can be heard either way.
What both readings share is the moment he said it: with the dirt in front of him, before he knew how the story would end.

how: Jewish teaching on bitachon, trust in God, runs from Proverbs and the Psalms to the gate of trust in Bachya ibn Pakuda's Duties of the Heart; some Jews repeat Nachum Ish Gamzu's words, gam zu l'tovah, this too is for the good.

o: the Hebrew root of strength and courage
the Hebrew root of hope and waiting
the Hebrew root of trust, and of safety

p: this too is for the good

s: in this root, trust and safety share letters
bitachon, trust; betach, safety: bet, tet, chet.
Nachum's chest reached the emperor full of jewels
it had been filled with dirt. he said it anyway: this too is for the good.
Jewish thinkers all define bitachon the same way
some say trust expects things to turn out well; others say it trusts whatever comes.

games.q: you're Nachum. you open the gift chest in front of the emperor, and it's full of dirt. what do you say?
o: this too is for the good.
I was robbed. it isn't my fault.
nothing. you close it and leave.
games.why: gam zu l'tovah. he said it before he knew the ending. the Talmud says the dirt turned out to be useful, and he came home honored.

practice: Let your shoulders drop, the way they would lying down in that psalm, and find one thing you've been carrying alone: a task, a worry, a question you haven't asked.

Picture one person who could hold part of it, see yourself handing it over, and notice what your hands feel like after. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep.

wordCard.voice: B-T-Ch. Bet, tet, chet: the root of bitachon, trust, and of betach, safety. Nachum's habit. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: trust, from bet, tet, chet, the same root as betach, safety.

carryVoice: Your line: trust. In Hebrew, the same letters spell safety, a place to lie down. Rest well.
